comments.text: The best postmortem I've seen was actually a conference talk: "Debugging Under Fire: Keep your Head when Systems have Lost their Mind" by Bryan Cantrill (in the GOTO conference, 2017) Here's a YouTube video of it: [VIDEO] Here's the slides: [LINK] It goes into detail about a pretty bad outage (when an entire data center was brought down), the human aspects, automation, how they handled it, the various risks, architectures, how things fail and about software development in general.

comments.why_zh: 操作员输错命令重启了整个数据中心
comments.quote_zh: 我强烈推荐 Bryan Cantrill 的演讲[1]，讲的是有一次操作员误操作重启了整个数据中心
comments.text_zh: > 我运营一个超过 10 年的 YouTube 频道，有超过 770,000 名订阅者、将近 600 个公开视频、120,000,000 次观看 当软件涉及管理一个在线、公开、大规模多用户的系统时，那些即时执行、常常悄无声息、且可能造成破坏的传统 Unix 风格命令，很容易让你搬起石头砸自己的脚。更糟的是，有些命令可能因为一个笔误就让你不小心把所有人的脚都打中。传统例子是不小心输入了类似 “rm -f * .bak” 的东西（注意星号后面多了一个空格）。关于这类问题的精彩讨论，我强烈推荐 Bryan Cantrill 的演讲[1]，讲的是有一次操作员因为一条输错的命令重启了整个数据中心。这个问题的一般解决方案是把合理性检查内建到软件里。用户刚刚要求重新格式化 500 台主机，但以前几乎所有使用“reformat”命令的情况影响的主机都不到 10 台。也许我们应该向真实的人请求确认，问他们是否真的打算运行这个异常具有破坏性的命令。为什么 YouTube 没有在自动下架/警告/频道删除工具里加入这种合理性检查？Google 写了自动化程序，可以决定删除一个有很长历史、许多成功视频的频道。为什么这个自动化程序没有基本的合理性检查，在执行异常具有破坏性的操作（比如删除一个有 10 年历史和大量内容记录的频道）时要求操作员输入？
comments.text: > I run a YouTube channel that is over 10 years old , has over 770,000 subscribers , almost 600 public videos , 120,000,000 views When writing software involved in managing a live, public, massively multi-user system, the traditional unix-style commands that are immediate, often silent, and capable of damaging effects become a really easy way to shoot yourself in the foot. Worse, some commands might let you accidentally shoot everyone's foot on a typo. The traditional example is accidentally typing something like "rm -f * .bak" (note the extra space after the star). For a good discussion of this type of problem, I highly recommend Bryan Cantrill's talk[1] about the time an operator accidentally rebooted an entire datacenter with a single miss-typed command. The general solution to this is building sanity checks into the software. The user just asked to reformat 500 hosts, but almost all previous uses olf the 'reformat' command affected less than 10 hosts. Maybe we should ask for verification from an actual human if they really intended to run this unusually destructive command. Why doesn't YouTube have this kind of sanity check in their automated takedown/strike/channel-deletion tools? Google wrote automation that can decide to delete a channel with a long history and many successful videos. Why doesn't that automation have basic sanity checks that ask for operator input when asked to do an unusually destructive action like deleting a 10 year old channel with a huge history?

comments.why_zh: 管理长时间故障，包括团队的睡眠管理
comments.quote_zh: Bryan Cantrill 有一个关于管理故障的精彩演讲
comments.text_zh: 我想这完全取决于，为了让业务最绝对必要的部分运转起来，需要把多少基础设施立起来。公司需要内部工单系统到位，才能处理外部客户交易吗？大概不需要，但最终会需要（所以也许把它挪到第二梯队恢复流程？）。我公司的 RTO 是 24 小时内恢复处理新客户交易。恢复旧交易肯定要更久，但至少新交易能继续。如果你自己公司的 RTO 是 2 周，那听起来需要到位的东西很多。业务连续性/灾难恢复的一部分，就是让管理层签字同意这类数字，不管大小。确保它们现实可行。你说得对，这种恢复一点都不好玩。Bryan Cantrill 有一个关于管理故障的精彩演讲（[VIDEO]）。我最大的收获之一是，如果你面对的是大面积故障和漫长的恢复过程，尽快和团队做好睡眠管理。累到半死的人更可能做出脑子坏掉的决策。
comments.text: I suppose it all depends on how much infra needs to be stood up for the absolute necessities of the business to operate. Does the company need that internal ticketing system in place to process external client transactions? Probably not, but it'll need it eventually (so maybe that moves to 2nd tier restore process?). My company's RTO is 24hrs to processing new client transactions. Restoring old ones will definitely take longer, but at least new ones can proceed. If your own company's RTO is 2w, that sounds like a lot needs to be in place. Part of the business continuity/ disaster recovery is getting management to sign off on those types of numbers, big or small. Make sure they're realistic. You're right that this type of recovery is not fun. Bryan Cantrill gives a great presentation about managing an outage ( [VIDEO] ). One of my biggest takeaways, if you're looking at a sweeping outage and a long haul of a recovery, do sleep management asap with your team. Dead tired people are more likely to make brain dead decisions.

comments.text_zh: > 我不确定你真是这样，因为你之前承认过自己至少有一部分是 sysadmin :) 哈哈！我真希望能想起那是哪场演讲。Bryan Cantrill 在他的一次演讲里有一句关于 DevOps 的妙语（我想是这一场：[VIDEO]）。大意是：“你可以说自己是 DevOps，但当事情搞砸时，你要么是 Dev，要么是 Ops。如果你是 Dev，你会想在重启故障机器之前先调试问题。如果你是 Ops，你会想尽快重启机器让它恢复。”从这个角度看，我肯定远远偏在 Dev 这一端；当某个东西灾难性地出错，而有人重启机器来‘解决问题’时，我的第一反应是‘你个混蛋，你把尸体烧了’ 整件事都太棘手了。回看我之前写的内容，我也意识到在某些方面我正在助长这种无知。我为团队搭了一套非常好的 Consul 和 Nomad 环境，所以他们基本上只要把 .wars 和 Docker 容器丢给集群，它们就会自动被调度到有空余容量的地方。负载均衡器、数据库集群、所有服务发现和作业调度相关的东西……他们从来不需要进去设置这些。也许该做更多指导了……总之，谢谢你让我思考这些。最近我因为看到太多人不知道自己构建的东西实际怎么运行，有点烦躁。你真是很棒的
comments.text: > I'm not sure you do, since you admitted to really being at least part sysadmin, earlier :) Hah! I wish I could remember which talk it was. Bryan Cantrill had a good line about DevOps in one of his talks (I think it was this one: [VIDEO] ). The gist was "you can say you're DevOps, but when the shit hits the fan, you're either going to be Dev or Ops. If you're a Dev, you're going to want to debug the problem before rebooting the failed machine. If you're Ops, you're going to want to reboot the machine as fast as you can to get it back up." Through that lens, I'm definitely pretty far over on the Dev spectrum; when something goes catastrophically wrong and someone reboots a box to "solve the problem", my first reaction is "YOU FUCKER YOU BURNED THE CORPSE" It's such a tricky thing all around. Looking back at what I wrote earlier, I also realize that in some ways I'm facilitating the ignorance. I've got a really nice Consul and Nomad setup for the team, so they can pretty much just toss .wars and Docker containers at the cluster and they'll automatically get scheduled somewhere with spare capacity. The load balancer, the database cluster, all of the service discovery and job scheduling stuff... they've never had to get in and set any of that up. Maybe it's time to do more mentoring... Anyway, thanks for getting me thinking. I've been a little bit grouchy lately about all of the recent experiences of people not knowing how the stuff they build actually runs. You've been a great

comments.quote_zh: 我记得 Bryan Cantrill 做过一个有趣的演讲
comments.text_zh: > 我只想说，如果 A-E 全在同一个网络上，你就必须依赖外部服务，因为该网络可能会挂掉。谢天谢地，如今在混合/多云环境中利用多个网络并不太难！不过，取决于所需的访问控制和审计，这种设置可能需要多花一点功夫。不过你确实提出了一个极好的点：这在许多系统里都是严重的单点故障，因为我个人也见过很多这样的设置（实际上是大多数）：我确实怀疑，在很多情况下这样做是为了易用/方便，即使它可能导致停机。当然，在某些情况下停机是可以接受的，所以我不能反驳说选择这种更简单的设置也可能有道理——例如，把自家公司开发环境用的应用/监控全放在同一个网络上。不过，如果这种拓扑在大规模下仍被保留，事情就会变得有点意思。类似地，我记得 Bryan Cantrill 做过一个有趣的演讲“Debugging Under Fire: Keep your Head when Systems have Lost their Mind”，讲的是重启他们整个数据中心以及这件事的影响：[VIDEO]
comments.text: > All I say is that you must relay on externals if A-E are all on the same network as it may go down. Thankfully, it's not too hard to take advantage of multiple networks in a hybrid/multi-cloud setup nowadays! Though, depending on the necessary access controls and auditing, such a setup might require slightly more work. You do bring up an excellent point, though, about how it's a serious single point of failure in many systems out there, because personally I've also seen many setups like that (the majority of them, actually): I do suspect that in many cases that is indeed done for ease of use/convenience, even if it may lead to downtime. Of course, in some cases downtime is acceptable, so I cannot argue that it can also make sense to choose such a simpler setup - for example, for having your own company's applications/monitoring for development environments all on the same network. Though if this topology is retained at scale, things can get a bit interesting. On a similar note, I recall Bryan Cantrill doing an interesting presentation "Debugging Under Fire: Keep your Head when Systems have Lost their Mind" that talked about restarting their whole data center and the implications of that: [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: 我是！（和合著者 Dave Pacheco 一起。）而且我仍然怀有梦想，希望有一天我们能把它写完：我们大概已经写了三分之一，但后来生活在各个方面横插一脚。确实，作为撰写我们这本书（我们给它起名为 The Joy of Debugging）准备工作的一部分，我们读了 Wheeler 的 Debugging。一方面，我认为只要有人写调试方面的东西就是好事，因为这个主题一直没有得到它应得的重视。但另一方面，这里的“方法论”其实更像是一堆格言警句；如果大家觉得有帮助，那很好——但我读完 Debugging 后的感觉是，关于调试的权威著作还有待写出。幸运的是，我和 Dave 的努力并没有白费：作为检验我们自己在这个主题上的想法的一部分，我在 2015 年到 2017 年左右做了一系列演讲，介绍了我们的思考。把这些内容大量整合在一起的一次演讲，是我 2017 年的 GOTO Chicago 演讲，讲的是调试生产系统。[0] 那次演讲并没有涵盖我们全部的思考，但我认为它涉及了其中很多内容——而且我确实认为它与 Wheeler 的工作形成了一定对比。[0] [VIDEO]
comments.text: I was! (Along with co-author Dave Pacheco.) And I still have the dream that we'll finish it one day: we had written probably a third of it, but then life intervened in various dimensions. And indeed, as part of our preparation to write our book (which we titled The Joy of Debugging ), we read Wheeler's Debugging . On the one hand, I think it's great to have anything written about debugging, as it's a subject that has not been treated with the weight that it deserves. But on the other, the "methodology" here is really more of a collection of aphorisms; if folks find it helpful, great -- but I came away from Debugging thinking that the canonical book on debugging has yet to be written. Fortunately, my efforts with Dave weren't for naught: as part of testing our own ideas on the subject, I gave a series of presentations from ~2015 to ~2017 that described our thinking. A talk that pulls many of these together is my GOTO Chicago talk in 2017, on debugging production systems.[0] That talk doesn't incorporate all of our thinking, but I think it gets to a lot of it -- and I do think it stands at a bit of contrast to Wheeler's work.
